college.stem: Baddeley and Hitch (1974) proposed working memory because a purely passive short-term store seemed too simple. A person keeps an intermediate result in mind while carrying out the next step of a calculation. Which feature of their proposal best accounts for this?
options: It combines temporary storage with active manipulation of information within a limited capacity.
It treats short-term memory as one passive store that needs no control processes at all.
It assigns every calculation to long-term memory and leaves only sensory traces in temporary storage.
It adds separate stores that remove any need to direct attention during complex tasks.
college.why: Working memory is a limited-capacity system for both temporary storage and manipulation, which is what holding a result while working on the next step requires. A purely passive store, the older short-term memory view, cannot explain the active operations.

simple.stem: How did Baddeley and Hitch (1974) define working memory?
options: A limited-capacity system that both stores and manipulates information for complex tasks.
A passive store that only holds information briefly, with no control processes.
A permanent store for all the facts and skills a person has learned.
A sensory store that keeps an exact copy of whatever was just seen.
simple.why: Working memory is a limited-capacity system for temporary storage and manipulation of information during tasks such as comprehension, learning and reasoning. The passive-store idea is the simpler short-term memory view it replaced.

college.stem: To multiply 43 by 6 mentally, a person computes 3 × 6 = 18, holds the 8, carries the 1, computes 6 × 4 = 24, adds the carried 1 to get 25, and combines 25 with the held 8 to reach 258. Which statement correctly separates storage from processing in this sequence?
options: Holding the 8 is storage, while carrying the 1 and adding it to 24 are active processing.
Carrying the 1 is passive storage, while holding the 8 is the only active processing step.
Only the final answer uses working memory, while every intermediate result goes to long-term memory.
Visualizing the digits rules out verbal processing, so the calculation needs no executive control.
college.why: The 8 simply has to stay available while other steps happen, which is storage; carrying, multiplying and adding change the information, which is active processing. The second option reverses the two roles.

simple.stem: When multiplying 43 by 6 in your head, which step is pure storage rather than active processing?
options: Holding the 8 in mind while working on the tens digit.
Carrying the 1 over so it can be added to the next product.
Multiplying 6 by 4 to get 24 in the second step.
Adding the carried 1 to 24 to get a total of 25.
simple.why: Holding the 8 only keeps a value available until it is needed, so it is storage. Carrying, multiplying and adding all change the numbers, so they are active processes.

college.stem: A student claims that Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) original working-memory model had four parts: a central executive, a phonological loop, a visuospatial sketchpad and an episodic buffer. Which correction is accurate?
options: The first three parts were in the 1974 model, and Baddeley added the episodic buffer in 2000.
The episodic buffer was in the 1974 model, and the central executive was added later in 2000.
The phonological loop replaced the visuospatial sketchpad in 2000 instead of working alongside it.
All four parts are different names for the single short-term store of the modal model.
college.why: The 1974 model had three components (central executive, visuospatial sketchpad, phonological loop); Baddeley added the episodic buffer as a fourth in 2000. The loop and sketchpad are separate, coexisting stores, not replacements or synonyms.

simple.stem: Which component did Baddeley add in 2000 to the working-memory model of Baddeley and Hitch (1974)?
options: The episodic buffer, which binds information into integrated episodes.
The central executive, which directs and maintains attention.
The phonological loop, which holds verbal and auditory information.
The visuospatial sketchpad, which holds visual and spatial information.
simple.why: The episodic buffer was added in 2000 as a fourth component. The central executive, phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad were all part of the original 1974 model.

college.stem: The phonological loop has two parts, the phonological store and the articulatory rehearsal process. Which statement correctly describes the division of labor between them?
options: The store holds verbal and auditory information, and rehearsal refreshes it so it does not decay.
The store holds visual locations, and rehearsal binds a meaningful story into one integrated episode.
The store suppresses irrelevant information, and rehearsal holds all long-term knowledge of language.
The store repeats speech aloud, and rehearsal permanently fixes the meaning of each repeated item.
college.why: The phonological store holds verbal and auditory information, and articulatory rehearsal keeps those items from decaying. Suppressing irrelevant information belongs to the central executive, and binding episodes belongs to the episodic buffer.

simple.stem: What does the articulatory rehearsal process do in the phonological loop?
options: It repeats verbal information so it does not decay from the phonological store.
It holds visual and spatial information such as shapes and locations.
It moves every repeated word permanently into long-term memory.
It directs attention and coordinates all the other working-memory components.
simple.why: Articulatory rehearsal repeats verbal items to keep them in the phonological store. Holding visual information is the sketchpad's job, and directing attention is the central executive's.

college.stem: A person silently repeats a short list of words while also keeping in mind the appearance and layout of a shape. How should these two kinds of temporary information be assigned to working-memory components?
options: The repeated words use the phonological loop, and the shape and its layout use the visuospatial sketchpad.
Both sit in the phonological store, because everything a person is aware of is coded verbally.
The shape uses the phonological loop, while the silently repeated words are held on the visuospatial sketchpad.
Both belong to the central executive, because the temporary stores hold only sounds heard aloud.
college.why: Verbal and auditory information is held in the phonological loop, and visual and spatial information in the visuospatial sketchpad. Silent rehearsal still uses the loop, and the central executive coordinates rather than stores every kind of content.

simple.stem: Which working-memory component holds visual and spatial information, such as the shape and location of objects?
options: The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information.
The phonological loop holds visual and spatial information.
The episodic buffer holds only visual and spatial information.
The central executive is the main store for visual shapes and locations.
simple.why: The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information. The phonological loop holds verbal and auditory information, and the central executive mainly directs attention and coordinates the stores.

college.stem: In Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) working-memory diagram, the central executive exchanges information with long-term knowledge in both directions, and the phonological loop and visuospatial sketchpad are also linked to it. A person solving a familiar sum combines a remembered arithmetic fact with digits currently held in mind. What do these links imply?
options: Previously learned information can be brought in and coordinated with temporary representations during the task.
Long-term knowledge can contribute only after all temporary processing on the task has finished.
Having a learned fact available makes the loop and the sketchpad unnecessary for any calculation.
Retrieving a familiar fact turns the central executive into a permanent storage site for that fact.
college.why: The model links working-memory components with long-term knowledge, and the central executive pulls information from long-term memory while a task is under way. Using a known fact does not remove the need for temporary maintenance or make the executive a permanent store.

simple.stem: In Baddeley and Hitch's (1974) model, how is working memory related to long-term knowledge?
options: Working memory can pull in and use information from long-term knowledge.
Working memory has no connection at all to long-term knowledge.
Long-term knowledge replaces working memory once a task becomes familiar.
Long-term knowledge is stored inside the phonological loop itself.
simple.why: The central executive pulls information from long-term memory, and the model's components are linked to long-term knowledge. Working memory is not cut off from long-term knowledge, nor replaced by it.

college.stem: In Conrad's (1964) study, letters were flashed briefly and participants then wrote them down. Errors tended to swap E with B rather than with F. Why is this error pattern informative?
options: The letters were held partly by sound, so a similar-sounding name competed despite a different shape.
The letters were heard rather than seen, so the errors simply reflect mishearing of the original items.
The most similar written shapes were confused, which supports a purely visual code for the letters.
Every letter was already stored permanently, and handwriting habits decided which letter was written.
college.why: E and B have similar spoken names, while E and F look alike. Sound-based errors after purely visual presentation show the letters were recoded and held by sound, not by a visual code alone.

simple.stem: In Conrad's (1964) study of briefly flashed letters, what kind of mistakes did participants usually make?
options: They confused letters that sound alike, such as E and B.
They confused letters that look alike, such as E and F.
They left out letters at random, with no pattern to their errors.
They wrote the right letters but always in reverse order.
simple.why: Participants rarely replaced a letter with one that looked like it but often replaced it with one that sounded like it. This is the phonological similarity effect, even though the letters were seen rather than heard.

college.stem: A researcher extends Conrad's (1964) flashed-letter procedure with two letter sets: one whose names sound alike but whose shapes differ, and one whose names sound distinct. Display time and recall instructions are the same for both. Which outcome would most directly support a sound-based code in memory?
options: More sound-based substitutions occur for the similar-sounding set, even with viewing conditions matched.
Whichever set is displayed for longer is remembered better, even though the amount of sound similarity stays the same.
Participants copy both sets accurately because the letters stay visible during the whole response.
Errors follow only how alike the written shapes are and never how the letters are pronounced.
college.why: The key manipulation is sound similarity with presentation conditions held constant, so extra sound-based errors for that set point to a phonological code. A display-time difference would be a confound, copying visible letters involves no memory, and shape-only errors would indicate a visual code.

simple.stem: Conrad (1964) compared memory for letters that sound alike with letters that do not. Which result shows that people hold letters by their sound?
options: More errors happen with the similar-sounding letters than with the distinct ones.
Equal numbers of errors happen with both sets of letters.
More errors happen only with letters that have similar shapes.
No errors happen with either set when letters are flashed.
simple.why: If letters are held by sound, letters with similar names should be confused more often. Equal errors, or errors driven by shape, would not point to a sound-based code.

college.stem: One student argues that the phonological loop is involved only when letters are heard, not when they are seen. Which finding from Conrad's (1964) study most directly challenges this claim?
options: Visually flashed letters were confused with letters that have similar spoken names, not mainly similar shapes.
Participants could identify a visible letter but could not keep it once the display had disappeared.
Letters that are seen and letters that are heard reach the senses in physically different forms.
Letters with different written shapes sometimes received different written responses from the participants in the study.
college.why: Sound-based confusions occurred even though the letters were shown visually, so the phonological loop must have converted the visual input into sound. Input modality and the code used to hold information can differ.

simple.stem: What did Conrad's (1964) study show about letters that are seen rather than heard?
options: Seen letters are still converted into sounds by the phonological loop.
Seen letters are stored only as visual shapes in the sketchpad.
Seen letters cannot be remembered once the display has disappeared.
Seen letters are confused only with other letters that look similar to them.
simple.why: Even visually presented letters were confused by sound, showing the phonological loop converts what is seen into a sound code. If they were held only as shapes, look-alike errors would dominate.

college.stem: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) found that lists of short words are recalled better than lists of long words. A student explains this by the shorter time needed to rehearse short words. Which observation fits that explanation?
options: Fewer long words than short words can be repeated within the brief time available for refreshing a list.
Long words always carry less meaning than short words, so they cannot enter working memory in the first place.
Short words bypass the phonological store and are held only as visual shapes on the sketchpad.
Recall of long words depends only on how many letters are visible, regardless of pronunciation.
college.why: Long words take longer to rehearse and to say during recall, so fewer fit into the time available for refreshing the list. The account is about pronunciation time, not meaning, visual storage or letter count.

simple.stem: Baddeley and colleagues (1975, 1984) described the word-length effect. What is it?
options: People remember more short words than long words from a list.
People remember more long words than short words from a list.
People remember words better when someone else reads the list aloud.
People remember the same number of words whatever their length.
simple.why: In the word-length effect, memory for lists is better for short words than for long words, because long words take longer to rehearse and to produce. The reverse pattern and a no-difference pattern are both wrong.

college.stem: Ellis and Hennelly (1980) found that Welsh–English bilingual children have a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English, although both tasks require remembering digits in order. Which interpretation explains the difference?
options: Welsh number names take longer to say, so fewer of them can be rehearsed within a brief interval.
The children have two fixed numerical capacities that are unrelated to the names used for the digits.
The English task measures visual memory, whereas the Welsh task measures only long-term knowledge.
The digits have different numerical values in the two languages, which changes how many are presented.
college.why: Welsh number words take longer to pronounce, so fewer can be rehearsed in the available time, which shortens span. Both tasks remain verbal digit recall, and the digits themselves do not change value.

simple.stem: Why did Welsh–English bilingual children have a shorter digit span in Welsh than in English (Ellis & Hennelly, 1980)?
options: Welsh number words take longer to pronounce than English ones.
The children had learned English numbers earlier than Welsh ones.
Welsh number words look more alike when they are written down.
The Welsh test used larger numbers than the English test did.
simple.why: Welsh numbers take longer to say, so fewer fit into rehearsal, which is the word-length effect applied to digits. The explanation is pronunciation time, not order of learning, spelling or number size.

college.stem: A student hears that a person's digit span is likely to equal the number of words they can say in 1.5–2.0 seconds and concludes that everyone's span is exactly two words. Which revision states the relationship correctly?
options: What matters is how many items can be spoken in that interval, so slower-to-say items reduce span.
The interval sets a fixed capacity of two items, no matter how quickly the items can be spoken.
The interval is the time needed to move every remembered word into permanent long-term storage.
The relationship holds only for visual shapes, because the spoken forms of items have no effect on digit span.
college.why: The time window limits how much can be rehearsed, not a fixed count of items: short, quickly spoken items fit more often than long ones. That is why word length and number-name duration change span.

simple.stem: A person's digit span is likely to equal the number of words they can say in about 1.5–2.0 seconds. What follows from this?
options: Words that take longer to say will lower how many can be remembered.
Everyone can remember exactly two words, regardless of word length.
How fast a person speaks has no effect on how many words can be remembered.
Only visual items, not spoken words, can be held for about 1.5–2.0 seconds.
simple.why: If span is set by how much can be said in a fixed time, slower-to-say words mean fewer items fit. The interval is a time limit, not a fixed two-word limit.

college.stem: Participants memorize lists of short and long words either in silence or while speaking continuously (articulatory suppression). Which pattern of results is expected?
options: Speaking lowers overall recall and shrinks the usual recall advantage for short words.
Speaking raises overall recall and enlarges the short-word advantage by adding extra rehearsal.
Speaking leaves recall unchanged because producing speech draws only on the visuospatial sketchpad.
Speaking changes only how the final answers are pronounced and cannot affect maintenance of the list.
college.why: Speaking occupies the articulatory rehearsal process, so recall gets worse and the word-length effect is reduced. Speech uses the phonological loop, not the sketchpad, and it does not add useful rehearsal.

simple.stem: What is articulatory suppression, and what does it do to memory?
options: Speaking while memorizing, which keeps the loop busy and makes recall worse.
Speaking while memorizing, which adds extra rehearsal and makes recall better.
Staying silent while memorizing, which blocks the sketchpad and makes recall worse.
Pointing while memorizing, which frees the loop and makes recall better.
simple.why: Articulatory suppression means speaking while memorizing; it keeps the phonological loop busy, so rehearsal is disrupted and memory is reduced. It does not help rehearsal.

college.stem: Visually presented letter lists normally produce confusions between similar-sounding letters. When participants speak while memorizing, this sound-similarity difference becomes smaller, yet overall recall worsens. Which explanation accounts for both changes?
options: Speaking occupies rehearsal and the recoding of letters into sound, lowering recall and the similarity effect.
Speaking increases memory capacity but leads participants to report fewer letters on purpose.
The smaller similarity effect shows that the visible letters never reached the senses in the first place.
Speaking makes the phonological store more accurate while leaving the rehearsal process fully free.
college.why: Articulatory suppression keeps the phonological loop busy, so letters are rehearsed and converted into sound less well; recall drops and sound-based confusions matter less. A smaller effect here reflects a disrupted process, not better memory.

simple.stem: What happens to the phonological similarity effect when people speak while memorizing letters?
options: The effect gets smaller because the phonological loop is kept busy.
The effect gets larger because speaking adds sound-based rehearsal.
The effect stays the same because speaking uses only the sketchpad.
The effect reverses, so similar-looking letters are confused instead.
simple.why: Articulatory suppression reduces both the phonological similarity effect and the word-length effect because the loop is occupied by speaking. Speaking does not add useful rehearsal or rely on the sketchpad.

college.stem: A researcher wants to test whether the recall advantage for short words depends on articulatory rehearsal. Which design addresses that question most directly while keeping the word lists comparable?
options: Cross word length with the presence or absence of a concurrent speaking task, using matched presentation.
Show long words for longer and short words for shorter durations, then compare recall of the two resulting lists.
Compare one group recalling word lists with a different group judging whether shapes are rotated.
Measure pronunciation speed in one language and use another group's visual accuracy as digit span.
college.why: Crossing word length with suppression tests whether the short-word advantage shrinks when rehearsal is blocked. The other designs add exposure-time confounds, unrelated tasks or different participant groups.

simple.stem: To test whether the word-length effect depends on rehearsal, what should a researcher compare?
options: Short and long word lists, each learned with and without speaking aloud.
Short word lists only, each learned both with and without speaking aloud.
Long word lists shown briefly and short word lists shown for longer.
Word lists learned by one group and shapes learned by another group.
simple.why: Both word lengths are needed to measure the word-length effect, and the speaking manipulation shows whether that effect depends on rehearsal. Using one length only, or unequal display times, cannot answer the question.

college.stem: Which pairing correctly matches each working-memory component with the kind of content it maintains?
options: The sketchpad maintains an object's shape and layout, while the loop maintains the sounds of a word list.
The sketchpad directs all of attention, while the loop maintains an object's visual shape and spatial layout.
The sketchpad maintains the sounds of a word list, while the loop suppresses irrelevant responses.
The sketchpad binds a story with knowledge, while the loop stores that same story permanently.
college.why: The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information, and the phonological loop holds verbal and auditory information. Directing attention and suppressing responses are executive functions, and binding with knowledge is the episodic buffer's role.

simple.stem: Which mental activity relies most on the visuospatial sketchpad?
options: Forming a visual image of an object in your mind.
Silently repeating a phone number to keep it in mind.
Switching attention back and forth between two tasks.
Recalling the meaning of a word learned years ago.
simple.why: The visuospatial sketchpad holds visual and spatial information and is involved in visual imagery. Repeating a number uses the phonological loop, and switching attention is a central executive function.

college.stem: In Brooks's (1968) sentence experiment, participants memorized a sentence and then indicated for each word whether it was a noun. Why was pointing easier than speaking these judgments?
options: The sentence occupied the phonological loop, so spoken answers competed with it while pointing did not.
Pointing rehearsed the sounds of the sentence more effectively than any spoken response could.
The sentence was stored only as a spatial outline on the sketchpad, which made spoken answers impossible to produce.
Speaking is harder than pointing in every task, whatever information is being remembered.
college.why: The phonological loop was busy with the sentence, so spoken responses competed for it, while the sketchpad was free for pointing. The F task shows speaking is not harder in general.

simple.stem: In Brooks's (1968) sentence experiment, which way of responding was easier, and why?
options: Pointing, because the phonological loop was busy with the sentence.
Speaking, because the visuospatial sketchpad was busy with the sentence.
Pointing, because the sketchpad was busy with the sentence.
Speaking, because the phonological loop was free during the task.
simple.why: Pointing was easier because the sentence kept the phonological loop busy, leaving the sketchpad free for a pointing response. A sentence is verbal, so it does not occupy the sketchpad.

college.stem: A research team repeats Brooks's (1968) sentence task with the same sentences and the same noun judgments, changing only whether answers are spoken or given by pointing. What does this comparison test?
options: Whether changing the response mode changes interference with the same verbal memory load.
Whether sentences with easier meanings always increase the number of stored visual objects.
Whether the noun judgments disappear when participants are given a longer retention interval.
Whether participants become more accurate because they can look back at the sentence.
college.why: Holding the sentence and the judgment constant isolates the effect of response mode on interference. The design does not vary meaning or delay, and the sentence is held in memory rather than visible.

simple.stem: In Brooks's (1968) sentence experiment, what was the one thing that differed between the two conditions?
options: Whether participants gave their answers by speaking or by pointing.
Whether participants memorized a sentence or memorized a shape.
Whether the sentence was displayed for a short or a long time.
Whether participants judged the nouns or the verbs in the sentence.
simple.why: Both conditions used a memorized sentence and noun judgments; only the response changed (speaking versus pointing). The sentence-versus-shape contrast comes from comparing this study with the F task.

college.stem: In Brooks's (1968) F task, participants held an F-shaped outline in mind and judged each successive corner as an inside or an outside corner. Which statement gives the result and its explanation?
options: Speaking was easier, because pointing added a spatial demand while the sketchpad was busy with the shape.
Pointing was easier, because the shape occupied the phonological loop and left spatial processing unused.
Speaking was easier, because the shape and the spoken labels were both held in one verbal component.
Pointing was easier, because it removed the need to remember the shape before judging the corners.
college.why: The remembered F occupied the visuospatial sketchpad, so pointing competed with it while speaking could use the free phonological loop. This is the opposite of the sentence result.

simple.stem: In Brooks's (1968) F task, which way of responding was easier, and why?
options: Speaking, because the sketchpad was busy with the image of the F.
Pointing, because the sketchpad was busy with the image of the F.
Speaking, because the phonological loop was busy with the image of the F.
Pointing, because the phonological loop was free during the task.
simple.why: Speaking was easier because the image of the F kept the sketchpad busy, while the phonological loop was free for spoken answers. A visual image does not occupy the phonological loop.

college.stem: In the pointing condition of Brooks's (1968) F task, participants pointed to OUT or IN on a response sheet for each corner of the remembered outline. A student assumes the sheet already shows the correct answer for each corner. Which description of the task is accurate?
options: OUT and IN are only response choices, and each corner must be judged from the shape held in mind.
Each row states the correct answer, so the participant can finish without remembering the shape.
The sheet turns the F into a verbal sentence, which removes the visual and spatial memory demand.
Each response refers to a newly displayed corner, so there is no remembered outline to follow.
college.why: Every row offers the same two alternatives, OUT and IN, as places to point; the answer has to come from mentally tracing the remembered F. The sheet adds a spatial response demand rather than giving the solution.

simple.stem: In Brooks's (1968) F task, what did participants have to do for each corner of the F?
options: Judge from memory whether it was an inside or an outside corner.
Copy the corner while the F stayed visible in front of them.
Name aloud the letter that the corner looked most like.
Count how many corners the F had before giving any answer at all.
simple.why: Participants memorized the F and then indicated, corner by corner, whether each was an inside or outside corner. The F was held in mind, not copied from view.

college.stem: Brooks (1968) found pointing easier when a sentence was being remembered but speaking easier when an F shape was being remembered. Which conclusion accounts for this reversal?
options: Interference depends on whether the response and the remembered information compete for the same verbal or visuospatial resources.
Pointing is easier in every memory task, but participants reversed the instructions for the shape task.
A single passive store is disrupted to the same degree by every possible way of making a response.
The response advantage depends entirely on whether the correct answer for each item is yes or no.
college.why: Tasks are easier when the held information and the response use different types of short-term memory, which is why the advantage flips with the type of content. This supports partly separate verbal and visuospatial capacities, not a fixed ranking of responses.

simple.stem: What general conclusion follows from Brooks's (1968) sentence and F experiments?
options: Tasks are easier when the memory and the response use different types of short-term memory.
Tasks are easier when the memory and the response use the same type of short-term memory.
Pointing is always an easier way to respond than speaking aloud.
Speaking is always an easier way to respond than pointing.
simple.why: Pointing was easier for the sentence and speaking was easier for the F, so the easier response is the one that uses the other type of short-term memory. Neither response is always easier.

college.stem: A researcher claims that Brooks's (1968) sentence result shows speaking is always harder than pointing. Which additional condition would test this claim most strongly?
options: Have participants judge inside and outside corners of a remembered F, comparing spoken and pointing responses.
Repeat the same sentence task, but use speaking as the only response condition in the study.
Make every sentence longer while also giving participants more time to point at their answers.
Remove the memory demand entirely and ask participants which way of responding they prefer.
college.why: The F task changes the remembered information to visuospatial and reverses the advantage, which directly refutes a general speaking disadvantage. Testing speaking alone, or changing length and timing together, cannot show a reversal.

simple.stem: Brooks (1968) found pointing easier for a remembered sentence. What happened when participants remembered an F shape instead?
options: The result reversed, and speaking became easier than pointing.
Pointing stayed easier, just as it had been for the remembered sentence.
Speaking and pointing became equally hard for participants.
Participants could not remember the F well enough to respond.
simple.why: With the F, speaking was easier than pointing, the opposite of the sentence result. The sketchpad was busy with the image, while the phonological loop was free.

college.stem: In one task a person holds a sentence in mind while responding; in another, the person holds a mental image of a shape while responding. Based on Brooks's (1968) findings, which pairing of response modes should produce the least interference?
options: Pointing while holding the sentence, and speaking while holding the image of the shape.
Speaking while holding the sentence, and pointing while holding the image of the shape.
Speaking for both tasks, because producing language never uses any temporary processing.
Pointing for both tasks, because spatial responses never compete with mental images.
college.why: Interference is lowest when the response uses a different type of short-term memory from the held content: pointing for verbal content, speaking for visual content. The sentence and F results show opposite advantages, so neither single mode is best for both.

simple.stem: Someone holds a mental picture of a map while answering questions about it. Based on Brooks (1968), which way of answering would interfere least?
options: Answering out loud, since speech uses the phonological loop instead.
Pointing to locations, since pointing uses the phonological loop.
Pointing to locations, since the sketchpad is free during mental imagery.
Answering out loud, since speech uses the visuospatial sketchpad.
simple.why: A mental map occupies the visuospatial sketchpad, so a spoken answer, which uses the phonological loop, interferes least. Pointing is spatial and would compete with the image, as in the F task.

college.stem: Verbal and visuospatial short-term memory are considered somewhat independent of each other. Which interpretation states that claim at the right strength?
options: The two have at least partly separate capacities, so interference depends on the kinds of information and operations involved.
The two systems can never interact with each other or with executive control during any task.
Each system gains unlimited capacity whenever the other system is also being used at the same time.
All temporary representations are identical, so the type of task cannot affect how much interference occurs.
college.why: Somewhat independent means at least separate capacities, which is why interference depends on whether tasks share a type of memory. It does not mean complete isolation, since the central executive coordinates both, nor unlimited capacity.

simple.stem: What does it mean that verbal and visuospatial short-term memory are somewhat independent?
options: They have at least partly separate capacities that can be used together.
They are one system that shares a single capacity for everything.
They never interact with each other or with the central executive.
Each of them has an unlimited capacity of its own.
simple.why: Somewhat independent means they have at least separate capacities, so verbal and visual tasks interfere less with each other. They still interact, coordinated by the central executive, and neither has unlimited capacity.

college.stem: Shepard and Metzler (1971) asked participants to judge whether two block figures shown at different orientations were the same object. For picture-plane pairs, reaction time rose roughly linearly with the angle between the figures. Which account best fits this relation?
options: A larger angle requires more mental rotation before the two figures can be compared in alignment.
A larger angle speeds the judgment because less visual information has to be held in mind.
Reaction time is unrelated to rotation, because the measure counts how many words are recalled.
Every orientation is recognized instantly, and the times only reflect how fast figures are named.
college.why: Reaction time increases steadily with angle, consistent with mentally rotating a spatial representation step by step until the figures line up. Faster judgments at larger angles or instant recognition would not produce a rising line.

simple.stem: In Shepard and Metzler's (1971) mental rotation study, how did reaction time change as the angle of rotation increased?
options: Reaction time increased steadily as the angle got larger.
Reaction time decreased steadily as the angle got larger.
Reaction time stayed the same at every angle tested.
Reaction time rose only once the angle passed 180 degrees.
simple.why: For picture-plane pairs, reaction time rose in a near-straight line from about 0 to 180 degrees. Larger rotations took longer, which suggests a mental rotation process.

college.stem: Two pairs of block figures like those used by Shepard and Metzler (1971) are matched in construction but differ in picture-plane rotation: one pair is 20 degrees apart and the other 160 degrees apart. Which prediction follows from their results?
options: The 160-degree pair should generally take longer to judge than the 20-degree pair.
The 160-degree pair should generally take less time to judge than the 20-degree pair.
Both pairs should take the same time, because the objects themselves are held constant.
Only the number of digits a participant can remember should change with the angle.
college.why: Reaction time increases with angular separation, so the larger rotation should take longer. Matching the objects does not remove the extra mental rotation that a larger angle requires.

simple.stem: Based on Shepard and Metzler (1971), which pair of rotated figures should take longest to compare?
options: A pair rotated 160 degrees apart from each other.
A pair rotated 20 degrees apart from each other.
A pair rotated 60 degrees apart from each other.
A pair that is not rotated apart from each other at all.
simple.why: Reaction time rises with the angle of rotation, so the 160-degree pair takes longest. An unrotated pair is the fastest to compare.

college.stem: A researcher proposes that comparing picture-plane pairs in Shepard and Metzler's (1971) task involves no time-consuming spatial transformation. With the objects and the judgment kept comparable, which result would most directly challenge this proposal?
options: Judgment time increases systematically as the angle between the two objects increases.
Participants report that the block figures look unfamiliar before the task begins.
One display has more objects and also allows participants a longer time to respond.
Participants accurately name a letter while it is visible, with no orientation judgment.
college.why: A systematic rise in time with angle is the signature of a transformation that takes longer the farther it must go. Familiarity reports, confounded displays and unrelated naming tasks do not isolate rotation time.

simple.stem: What did Shepard and Metzler's (1971) results suggest people do when comparing rotated objects?
options: They mentally rotate one object, which takes longer for larger angles.
They recognize every orientation instantly, without any mental transformation.
They name each object aloud and then compare the names instead.
They memorize every object at every possible angle in advance.
simple.why: Because reaction time grows with the angle, people appear to rotate a mental image until the objects line up. Instant recognition would give the same time at every angle.

college.stem: Shepard and Metzler (1971) used both picture-plane rotation and depth rotation. Which statement correctly distinguishes the two?
options: Picture-plane rotation turns an object within the flat viewing plane, while depth rotation turns it in three dimensions.
Picture-plane rotation changes an object's color, while depth rotation changes how many blocks it contains.
Picture-plane rotation repeats an object's verbal label, while depth rotation stores its sound without an image.
Picture-plane rotation moves the response button, while depth rotation moves attention away from the object.
college.why: The distinction is about the axis of rotation: within the plane of the picture versus through depth. Color, block count, verbal labels and response buttons are not what differs between the two.

simple.stem: In Shepard and Metzler's (1971) study, what is depth rotation?
options: Turning an object in three dimensions rather than within the flat picture.
Turning an object only within the flat surface of the picture.
Making an object larger or smaller on the display screen.
Moving an object closer to or farther from the viewer.
simple.why: Depth rotation turns the object through three-dimensional space, while picture-plane rotation turns it within the flat picture. Changing size or distance is not rotation.

college.stem: During a mental calculation, a person replaces an old running total with a new one, switches from multiplying to adding, and ignores a nearby conversation. Which executive functions identified by Miyake and colleagues (2000) correspond to these three demands?
options: Updating the held information, shifting between operations, and inhibiting irrelevant information.
Storing a visual trace, permanently learning a fact, and lengthening the duration of sensory input.
Phonological storage, visuospatial storage, and episodic storage, without any control operation.
Repeating the same total, keeping the same operation, and letting every distraction into memory.
college.why: Replacing the total is updating, switching operations is shifting, and ignoring the conversation is inhibition. The other options name storage or sensory processes, not executive control.

simple.stem: Miyake and colleagues (2000) split the central executive into three functions. What are they?
options: Updating information, shifting between tasks, and inhibiting distractions.
Storing sounds, storing images, and binding them together into episodes.
Encoding, storing, and retrieving information in long-term memory.
Seeing, hearing, and touching incoming sensory information.
simple.why: The central executive is often split into updating, shifting and inhibition (Miyake et al., 2000). Storing sounds and images belongs to the loop and sketchpad, not the executive.

college.stem: The central executive is often criticized as theorizing a 'homunculus' in the brain. Miyake and colleagues (2000) split executive control into updating, shifting and inhibition. How does this split respond to the criticism?
options: It names specific control operations instead of giving all control to one unexplained inner agent.
It establishes that an actual miniature person directs each of the working-memory components.
It replaces the phonological store with three separate permanent stores for unrelated kinds of knowledge.
It removes the need to explain attention, because all contents are selected automatically.
college.why: The homunculus criticism is that calling something an executive names a controller without explaining how it works. Splitting it into distinct operations specifies what the control consists of, rather than positing a literal little person.

simple.stem: Why is the idea of a central executive often criticized?
options: It can sound like a little person in the brain doing the work.
It cannot hold any verbal information such as words or numbers.
It was added to the model late, in the year 2000.
It holds only visual images and ignores every other kind of information.
simple.why: The central executive is criticized as theorizing a homunculus, a little person in the head who does the work without explanation. It was part of the original 1974 model; the episodic buffer was the 2000 addition.

college.stem: A participant can repeat a verbal list accurately but struggles to keep unrelated information from intruding while using that list. Which function is most directly implicated in the difficulty?
options: Executive inhibition, which suppresses irrelevant information while held contents are being used.
The visual appearance of the list before any information has reached the sensory system.
Permanent storage of the exact list in memory for the rest of the participant's life.
A single process in which verbal maintenance and attentional control are really one and the same operation.
college.why: Repeating the list is phonological rehearsal, which works; suppressing irrelevant information is a central executive function (inhibition). Maintenance and executive control are separate demands.

simple.stem: Which part of working memory controls the suppression of irrelevant information?
options: The central executive, which directs attention and suppresses distractions.
The phonological store, which holds verbal and auditory information.
The visuospatial sketchpad, which holds visual and spatial information.
The articulatory rehearsal process, which repeats words aloud or silently to prevent decay.
simple.why: The central executive directs and maintains attention and controls suppression of irrelevant information. The stores and the rehearsal process hold or refresh information but do not filter it.

college.stem: Baddeley (2000) added the episodic buffer partly because people can immediately recall far more words from a meaningful sentence than from a list of unrelated words. Which proposed function addresses that difference?
options: Binding temporary verbal and visuospatial contents with long-term knowledge into integrated episodes.
Holding every word as a separate item without drawing on any existing knowledge of language.
Replacing long-term memory with a temporary visual image of the entire sentence.
Removing the capacity limit of the phonological store whenever a sentence is grammatical.
college.why: The buffer binds information from the loop, sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes, so knowledge of meaning lets many words be held as a few units. Holding words as separate items would predict ordinary unrelated-word span.

simple.stem: What does the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000) do?
options: It binds information from the loop, sketchpad, and long-term memory into episodes.
It holds only the sounds of words so that they can be rehearsed.
It directs attention and switches between different tasks.
It stores every experience permanently with unlimited capacity.
simple.why: The episodic buffer is a limited-capacity store that binds information from the phonological loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. Directing attention belongs to the central executive.

college.stem: A person immediately recalls about 16 words of a meaningful sentence. A student concludes that the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000) cannot be limited to about four chunks. Which response reconciles the two facts?
options: A single chunk can group several related words, so recalled words can outnumber the integrated units.
A chunk is always exactly one word, so a sentence longer than four words could never be recalled immediately.
Meaningful sentences bypass temporary memory and are never available for immediate recall at all.
Recalling sixteen words shows that every form of temporary storage has unlimited capacity.
college.why: Chunks are meaningful units, not single words, so about four chunks can hold a much longer sentence. The limited capacity and the 16-word recall are therefore compatible.

simple.stem: What is the approximate capacity of the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000)?
options: About 4 chunks of integrated information.
About 16 separate, unrelated words at once.
About 7 plus or minus 2 single letters.
An unlimited amount of information at once.
simple.why: The episodic buffer has a limited capacity of about four chunks. About 16 words is how much of a meaningful sentence people recall, which is possible because each chunk can hold several words.

college.stem: Some amnesic patients can immediately recall a story they have just heard. Which part of Baddeley's (2000) episodic-buffer account most directly addresses this observation?
options: An integrated episode can be held temporarily even when longer-term memory is impaired.
Immediate recall proves that every long-term memory function is intact in all amnesic patients.
The story must be held only as isolated speech sounds with no meaningful links among them.
The episodic buffer permanently repairs the long-term memory impairment each time a story is heard.
college.why: Immediate story recall in amnesia suggests a temporary store that holds integrated episodes, which is the buffer's role. It does not imply intact long-term memory or a permanent repair.

simple.stem: Which observation helped motivate adding the episodic buffer (Baddeley, 2000)?
options: Some amnesic patients can immediately recall a story they just heard.
People confuse letters that sound alike even when they see them.
People remember fewer long words than short words from a list.
Reaction time increases as two objects are rotated farther apart from each other.
simple.why: Immediate story recall by some amnesic patients, together with recall of about 16 words of a meaningful sentence, motivated the buffer. The other findings support the phonological loop and the sketchpad.

college.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) task, an arrow cue was followed by a brief memory display of red bars, sometimes with blue bars added as irrelevant items, then a blank delay and a test display. What did participants need to retain across the delay?
options: The orientations of the relevant red bars on the cued side, ignoring the blue bars.
Every visible bar equally, because the blue bars were extra targets in the distractor condition.
Only the color name of each bar, because the test never concerned the bars' orientations.
Nothing from the memory display, because it stayed visible throughout the test display.
college.why: The cue picks the relevant side, and the red bars there are the items to remember; blue bars are distractors to be filtered out. The memory display disappears during the delay, so the targets must be held in mind.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) task, what were the blue bars?
options: Irrelevant distractors that participants were supposed to ignore.
Extra targets that participants had to remember as well.
Cues that showed which side of the screen to attend.
Feedback signals telling participants that their previous answer was correct.
simple.why: The red bars were the items to remember, and the blue bars were irrelevant distractors. The cue showing which side to attend was an arrow.

college.stem: Why did Vogel and colleagues' (2005) procedure include a blank retention interval between the brief memory display and the test display?
options: The bars had to be held while absent, so memory-related activity could be measured after visual exposure ended.
The interval let participants copy the original bars while the memory display was still visible.
The interval turned the irrelevant blue bars into relevant red targets before each response.
The interval ensured that every participant had exactly the same working-memory capacity.
college.why: During the retention interval the screen is blank, so any later comparison depends on information held in working memory, and the activity recorded then reflects maintenance. A delay neither allows copying nor equalizes capacity.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) task, what happened during the retention interval?
options: The screen was blank, so participants had to hold the bars in mind.
The bars stayed on the screen so participants could keep looking at them.
Participants named each bar's color out loud to rehearse it.
A new set of bars appeared for participants to compare.
simple.why: The memory display was replaced by a blank screen (about 900 ms), so the bars had to be held in working memory until the test display. Brain activity continued well into this interval.

college.stem: Vogel and colleagues (2005) compared a display of two red targets with a display of two red targets plus two irrelevant blue bars. What is held constant, and what extra demand is added?
options: The number of relevant targets stays the same, while the distractor display adds a need to filter out irrelevant objects.
The total number of objects stays the same, while the distractor display removes every selection demand.
The number of relevant targets doubles, while the distractor display adds no irrelevant objects at all.
The memory demand disappears entirely, while the distractor display measures only the naming of colors.
college.why: Both displays require remembering two targets, so the added blue bars test exclusion of irrelevant items rather than a larger relevant load. The total number of objects is what changes.

simple.stem: Vogel and colleagues (2005) added two blue distractors to two red targets. What did this addition test?
options: How well participants could filter out irrelevant items.
How many more targets participants could remember.
How quickly participants could name the colors shown.
How long participants could look at the display.
simple.why: Adding distractors while keeping two targets tests filtering, that is, keeping irrelevant items out of working memory. A test of how many targets can be held would add relevant items instead.

college.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) high-capacity group, brain activity for two targets plus two distractors resembled activity for two targets alone rather than for four targets. Which inference fits?
options: High-capacity participants filtered out the distractors instead of holding every visible object in memory.
High-capacity participants held every distractor, producing the same load as four relevant objects.
High-capacity participants never registered the memory display and responded without any target information.
The two-target and four-target conditions placed identical memory loads on every participant.
college.why: Adding distractors had no effect for high-capacity people, so they kept only the relevant items in memory. Their activity was greater for four relevant items, so the two-item match is not a failure to register load.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) study, what happened to high-capacity participants' brain activity when blue distractors were added?
options: It stayed about the same as with the two red targets alone.
It rose to about the level seen with four red targets.
It dropped well below the level seen with two targets.
It disappeared completely during the blank retention interval.
simple.why: For high-capacity people, adding irrelevant blue items had no effect on activity. Low-capacity people were the ones whose activity increased.

college.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) low-capacity group, adding blue distractors to two relevant red items increased memory-related activity toward the level seen with four relevant items. Which account explains this?
options: Irrelevant items were let into working memory, using up resources alongside the two targets.
The distractors improved selection so much that fewer objects were processed than with two targets.
The relevant red items physically vanished from the screen as soon as blue items were added.
The larger response shows low-capacity people remembered the targets better than the high group.
college.why: The increase indicates poorer filtering: distractors entered working memory and added to the load. A larger load signal does not mean better memory for the targets.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) study, what happened for low-capacity participants when blue distractors were added?
options: Brain activity increased, as if they were also storing the distractors.
Brain activity stayed the same, as if they ignored the distractors.
Brain activity decreased, as if they had stopped storing the red targets.
Brain activity stopped, as if they had forgotten the whole display.
simple.why: Adding irrelevant blue items increased activity for low-capacity people, suggesting the distractors were held along with the targets. Activity staying the same was the high-capacity pattern.

college.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) EEG plots, negative voltage is plotted upward. A student assumes that a higher trace means a more positive voltage and therefore better memory. Which interpretation is correct?
options: A higher trace is a larger negative response, and whether targets or distractors drive it matters.
Plotting upward guarantees a positive voltage and therefore accurate recall of every target.
The sign of the plotted voltage reveals whether a bar on the screen was red or blue.
Every condition that produces a larger deflection must contain only relevant items and never any distractors.
college.why: The y-axis has −2 µV at the top, so a higher trace is a more negative response. In the low-capacity group a higher trace came from distractors being processed, so it does not mean better memory.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) EEG graphs, which direction on the y-axis shows negative voltage?
options: Up, because −2 µV is marked at the top of the axis.
Down, because −2 µV is marked at the very bottom of the axis.
Down, because voltage always increases toward the top.
Neither, because the graph shows only reaction times in seconds.
simple.why: The axis is labeled −2 µV at the top and +2 µV at the bottom, so negative voltage is plotted upward. The x-axis is time in milliseconds, not reaction time.

college.stem: Which pair of conditions in Vogel and colleagues' (2005) task most directly tests filtering efficiency, rather than just the effect of adding more relevant targets?
options: Two relevant targets alone versus the same two relevant targets with irrelevant blue distractors.
Two relevant targets versus four relevant targets, with no distractors present in either condition.
A visible display copied immediately versus an unrelated verbal sentence recalled at a later time.
One target condition with a short delay versus another target condition with a longer exposure.
college.why: Keeping the number of targets constant while adding irrelevant objects isolates filtering. Two versus four targets measures relevant load instead, and changing delay or exposure adds confounds.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) study, which comparison shows how well someone filters out distractors?
options: Two red targets alone versus two red targets plus two blue bars.
Two red targets alone versus four red targets with no blue bars.
A short delay versus a long delay with the same red targets.
Four red targets versus four blue bars with no red targets.
simple.why: Holding two targets constant and adding blue bars shows whether the distractors get into memory. Comparing two with four red targets measures how activity changes with more relevant items.

college.stem: Vogel and colleagues (2005) reported that measured working-memory capacity is correlated with an EEG measure of filtering efficiency. Which statement gives the direction of this finding?
options: Participants with higher measured capacity tended to exclude irrelevant items more efficiently.
Participants with higher measured capacity tended to hold more irrelevant items at the cost of targets.
Participants with lower measured capacity always had the highest filtering-efficiency values.
Filtering efficiency was unrelated to capacity, because irrelevant items never appeared in the task.
college.why: People with higher capacity were also less distracted by irrelevant items, so capacity and filtering efficiency rise together. The opposite direction contradicts the scatterplot, and distractors were part of the task.

simple.stem: What did Vogel and colleagues (2005) find about people with high working-memory capacity?
options: They were better at ignoring the irrelevant items.
They stored more of the irrelevant blue items as well.
They were worse at ignoring the irrelevant items.
They showed no brain activity during the delay.
simple.why: Capacity was correlated with filtering efficiency: people with higher capacity were less distracted by irrelevant items. They did show activity during the delay, which grew with more relevant items.

college.stem: Two participants must hold the same number of relevant bars in mind. One also processes many irrelevant blue bars and recalls the targets less well. How does the filtering account of Vogel and colleagues (2005) interpret the lower score?
options: Irrelevant items can take up limited capacity, leaving less room for the relevant targets.
A low target score shows the participant had no memory-related electrical response at all.
A low target score means no relevant information ever reached the participant's eyes.
Extra irrelevant items must raise effective capacity, because more objects were on the screen.
college.why: Working memory is limited, so distractors that get in use capacity that the targets need. Differences in capacity may partly reflect how well people keep irrelevant items out, not sensory failure or absent activity.

simple.stem: Based on Vogel and colleagues (2005), why might someone have a lower working-memory capacity?
options: They let irrelevant items use up some of their limited capacity.
They see fewer of the items that appear on the screen in the first place.
They have no brain activity during the delay period.
They store the relevant items permanently instead of briefly.
simple.why: Lower-capacity people were more distracted by irrelevant items, which then took up limited working-memory space. They still saw the display and showed delay activity.

college.stem: A person recalls similar-sounding letters poorly, remembers fewer long words than short words, and does worse when speaking during memorization. Which labels match these three findings in order?
options: The phonological similarity effect, the word-length effect, and articulatory suppression, in that order.
The word-length effect, articulatory suppression, and the phonological similarity effect, in that order.
Articulatory suppression, the phonological similarity effect, and the word-length effect, in that order.
Mental rotation, episodic binding, and permanent long-term storage of the items, in that order.
college.why: Sound-based confusion is the phonological similarity effect, poorer memory for long words is the word-length effect, and worse memory while speaking is articulatory suppression. All three are evidence for the phonological loop.

simple.stem: What is the phonological similarity effect?
options: Letters or words that sound alike are easily confused in memory.
Letters or words that look alike are easily confused in short-term memory.
Short words are remembered better than long words in a list.
Speaking while memorizing makes it harder to remember a list.
simple.why: The phonological similarity effect is the confusion of letters or words that sound similar. The other options describe a visual confusion, the word-length effect and articulatory suppression.

college.stem: Short and long words differ strongly in recall during ordinary memorization, but the difference shrinks under articulatory suppression. Which additional result is needed to avoid interpreting the smaller difference as improved memory?
options: Overall recall is lower under suppression, even though the gap between word lengths is smaller.
The words are now stored permanently, so no recall measure is needed in the suppression condition.
Participants now remember every long word perfectly, because all rehearsal has stopped.
The original word lists have been replaced with unrelated visual shapes during suppression.
college.why: A smaller effect can come with worse overall performance; under suppression people remember less and the word-length effect is reduced. Showing lower overall recall rules out the idea that memory improved.

simple.stem: Under articulatory suppression, the word-length effect gets smaller. What happens to overall recall?
options: Overall recall gets worse when people speak while memorizing.
Overall recall gets better when people speak while memorizing.
Overall recall stays exactly the same as when memorizing in silence.
Overall recall improves for the long words but not for the short words.
simple.why: Speaking while memorizing keeps the phonological loop busy, so people get worse at remembering. The word-length effect shrinks because rehearsal is disrupted, not because memory improves.

college.stem: A proposed study compares sentence memory with spoken answers against shape memory with pointed answers and finds both difficult. Why would adding the other response mode within each memory task, as Brooks (1968) did, be useful?
options: It tests whether the easier response flips with the kind of remembered information, rather than comparing unlike tasks.
It guarantees that sentence memory and shape memory are equally difficult before either one is measured.
It removes the need to keep response instructions consistent across all of the conditions in the study.
It converts the visual memory task into a purely auditory task in every one of the conditions.
college.why: Brooks's evidence comes from comparing speaking and pointing within each type of content and finding the advantage reverses. That ties interference to shared processing rather than to an uncontrolled difference between two tasks.

simple.stem: Why did Brooks (1968) test both speaking and pointing within each memory task?
options: To see whether the easier response changed with the type of information held.
To make the sentence task and the F task exactly equal in difficulty.
To check whether participants generally preferred speaking or pointing.
To turn the F task into a verbal task for every participant.
simple.why: Testing both responses for each task showed that pointing was easier for the sentence and speaking was easier for the F. That reversal is what links interference to the type of short-term memory being used.

college.stem: A model has separate verbal and visuospatial stores but no way to represent their contents together with long-term knowledge. Which addition by Baddeley (2000) fills this gap?
options: A limited-capacity episodic buffer that binds those sources into integrated episodes.
An unlimited phonological store that replaces every other working-memory component.
A longer-lasting sensory trace that stores all meaningful episodes permanently.
A response rule that forbids verbal and visual information from being used in one task.
college.why: The episodic buffer binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory into integrated episodes. Enlarging one store or lengthening sensory traces does not provide that binding.

simple.stem: Which working-memory component links the phonological loop, the visuospatial sketchpad, and long-term memory (Baddeley, 2000)?
options: The episodic buffer, which binds them into integrated episodes.
The phonological store, which holds verbal and auditory information.
Sensory memory, which briefly holds raw input from the senses.
The articulatory rehearsal process, which repeats verbal items.
simple.why: The episodic buffer, added in 2000, binds information from the loop, the sketchpad and long-term memory. The phonological store and rehearsal process are parts of the loop itself.

college.stem: A student treats the strongest retention-interval response as the best memory performance in every condition. Which result from Vogel and colleagues (2005) most clearly challenges that view?
options: Low-capacity participants show increased activity when irrelevant blue items accompany the targets.
High-capacity participants show a stronger response to four relevant items than to two relevant items.
The memory display appears before the retention interval rather than after the test display.
The cue tells participants which side of the display is relevant before the memory display appears.
college.why: For low-capacity people, activity rose when distractors were added, reflecting irrelevant items being held rather than better target memory. The four-versus-two result is consistent with the student's view, so it cannot challenge it.

simple.stem: In Vogel and colleagues' (2005) study, does more brain activity during the delay always mean better memory?
options: No, because low-capacity people's activity rose when distractors were added.
Yes, because more activity always means more targets are remembered.
Yes, because high-capacity people always showed the most activity.
No, because brain activity was never measured during the delay.
simple.why: Low-capacity people showed more activity with distractors, which reflects holding irrelevant items, not better memory. Activity was measured and continued well into the delay.

college.stem: A follow-up to Vogel and colleagues' (2005) study compares two relevant items alone, four relevant items alone, and two relevant items plus distractors. What role does the four-item condition play in interpreting the distractor condition?
options: It gives a higher relevant-load benchmark for judging whether distractors produce activity like holding more objects.
It makes the distractors relevant in every condition, so they no longer need to be told apart from targets.
It ensures that all electrical activity occurs only while the memory display is physically on the screen.
It substitutes a verbal span test for the visual comparison and removes the retention interval entirely.
college.why: The four-item condition shows what activity looks like when more objects are genuinely held. A distractor response close to it suggests the irrelevant objects also entered working memory.

simple.stem: Why did Vogel and colleagues (2005) include a condition with four red targets?
options: To show what brain activity looks like when more items are truly stored.
To make the blue distractors count as targets in every condition.
To measure how quickly participants could name four different colors aloud.
To give participants an easier task than the two-item condition.
simple.why: The four-target condition shows the activity produced by holding more relevant items, so it can be compared with the two-targets-plus-distractors condition. Activity was greater for four relevant items than for two.

college.stem: A participant holds verbal information accurately but loses track of which operation to perform when the task changes. Which interpretation is most consistent with the working-memory model?
options: Accurate verbal maintenance can coexist with a problem in executive shifting between operations.
Accurate verbal maintenance guarantees that every one of the executive control operations is fully intact.
Shifting is the phonological store's passive retention of every sound heard in the room.
A change of task must be handled entirely by sensory memory, with no executive involvement.
college.why: The model separates storage of verbal content (the phonological loop) from executive operations such as shifting. Success at one does not guarantee the other.

simple.stem: Which executive function lets a person switch from one task or operation to another?
options: Shifting, which moves control between tasks or operations.
Updating, which replaces old information with new information.
Inhibition, which suppresses irrelevant or distracting information.
Rehearsal, which repeats verbal information to keep it active.
simple.why: Shifting is switching between tasks or operations. Updating changes the held contents, inhibition suppresses distraction, and rehearsal is part of the phonological loop rather than an executive function.
